name: Health and Nutrition
description: A comprehensive exploration of nutrition science covering macronutrients, micronutrients, hydration, dietary guidelines, sports nutrition, and global food systems for healthy adolescent lifestyles.

modules.title: Introduction to Nutrition
modules.objectives: Define nutrition and its importance to health, identify the six classes of nutrients, and use current federal dietary guidance to evaluate balanced, nutrient-dense food choices.
modules.readingNote: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services — current Dietary Guidelines for Americans and supporting resources.
modules.videoNote: GIIS — Module 1: Introduction to Nutrition lesson video.
modules.practiceNote: Review the current federal dietary guidance and identify two principles that could improve the provided or fictional food diary.
modules.assignment: Submit: an annotated three-day food diary and short explanation using provided, fictional, or anonymized data. Include: nutrient strengths, nutrient gaps, two realistic improvements, and citations to current federal guidance; calories, weight, diagnoses, and sensitive health details are not required. Evaluation: claims use specific diary evidence and accurately apply the six nutrient classes and nutrient-dense food guidance.

modules.title: Macronutrients: Carbohydrates
modules.titleZh: 宏量营养素：碳水化合物
modules.objectives: Identify types of carbohydrates (simple vs. complex, fiber), understand their role as the body's primary energy source, and evaluate healthy carbohydrate food choices.
modules.readingNote: Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health — Carbohydrates
modules.videoNote: GIIS — Module 2: Macronutrients: Carbohydrates lesson video.
modules.practiceNote: Identify five high-quality carbohydrate sources and five poor-quality sources from your diet
modules.assignment: Submit: a comparison report on simple and complex carbohydrate food sources. Include: the glycemic-index concept and its limits, fiber's role, three practical food swaps, and evidence from at least one qualified source. Evaluation: comparisons are accurate, each swap is justified, and the report avoids labeling single foods as universally good or bad.

modules.title: Macronutrients: Proteins
modules.objectives: Explain the structure and functions of protein, differentiate complete from incomplete protein sources, and explain why protein needs vary by age, body size, activity, growth, and health context.
modules.readingNote: Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health — The Nutrition Source: Protein
modules.videoNote: GIIS — Module 3: Macronutrients: Proteins lesson video.
modules.practiceNote: Identify your estimated daily protein needs and plan a high-protein meal that includes a complete protein source
modules.assignment: Submit: a calculation sheet and one-day meal plan for a provided fictional student profile. Include: a reasonable protein range from a qualified cited source, the calculation steps, an explanation of why needs vary, and diverse food sources; personal weight or medical information is not required. Evaluation: the calculation is traceable, the source is credible, and the meal plan reasonably fits the profile and module concepts.

modules.title: Macronutrients: Fats
modules.objectives: Classify dietary fats (saturated, unsaturated, trans), understand their health implications, and identify food sources of healthy fats. Students will connect concepts to safe practice, explain risks or benefits, and document evidence of understanding in the module assignment.
modules.readingNote: Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health — Fats and Cholesterol
modules.videoNote: GIIS — Module 4: Macronutrients: Fats lesson video.
modules.practiceNote: Analyze a food label for fat content and classify fats found in the product
modules.assignment: Submit: a practical guide to saturated, unsaturated, and trans fats. Include: definitions, food-source examples, health effects, and three justified substitutions that favor unsaturated fats when appropriate. Evaluation: the guide uses accurate course evidence, distinguishes fat types clearly, and gives realistic advice without recommending elimination of all dietary fat.

modules.title: Micronutrients: Vitamins
modules.objectives: Identify water-soluble and fat-soluble vitamins, their functions, food sources, and consequences of deficiency or excess. Students will connect concepts to safe practice, explain risks or benefits, and document evidence of understanding in the module assignment.
modules.readingNote: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements — Vitamins and Minerals
modules.videoNote: GIIS — Module 5: Micronutrients: Vitamins lesson video.
modules.practiceNote: Choose two vitamins and research their functions, deficiency symptoms, and best food sources
modules.assignment: Submit: a reference chart for four fat-soluble and four water-soluble vitamins. Include: major functions, several food sources, age-appropriate intake guidance from qualified sources, and risks of deficiency or excessive supplementation. Evaluation: all eight entries cite qualified evidence, categories are accurate, and the chart does not diagnose deficiencies or prescribe supplements.

modules.title: Micronutrients: Minerals
modules.objectives: Identify key dietary minerals (calcium, iron, potassium, sodium, zinc), their roles in body function, deficiency conditions, and food sources. Students will connect concepts to safe practice, explain risks or benefits, and document evidence of understanding in the module assignment.
modules.readingNote: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements — Minerals
modules.videoNote: GIIS — Module 6: Micronutrients: Minerals lesson video.
modules.practiceNote: Analyze your typical diet for calcium and iron intake adequacy
modules.assignment: Submit: a comparison of calcium, iron, and zinc for adolescent health. Include: functions, varied food sources, age-appropriate intake guidance from qualified sources, and consequences of inadequate or excessive intake. Evaluation: each mineral claim cites qualified evidence, individual needs are acknowledged, and no personal diagnosis or supplement prescription is made.

modules.title: Water & Hydration
modules.objectives: Explain water's roles in the body, understand daily hydration requirements, and recognize signs of dehydration and overhydration. Students will connect concepts to safe practice, explain risks or benefits, and document evidence of understanding in the module assignment.
modules.readingNote: Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health — Water
modules.videoNote: GIIS — Module 7: Water & Hydration lesson video.
modules.practiceNote: Track your fluid intake for 3 days and compare to daily recommended amounts
modules.assignment: Submit: a one-page hydration guide for a fictional teenager. Include: water's roles, factors that change fluid needs, early warning signs, a plan for routine activity, and when symptoms require adult or medical help. Evaluation: guidance is evidence-based, avoids one fixed target for everyone, and distinguishes routine hydration from special exercise or health needs.

modules.title: Energy Balance & Weight Management
modules.objectives: Explain energy balance and basal metabolic rate, evaluate growth-supporting approaches to health and weight, and recognize when a teenager should seek guidance from a parent, guardian, or qualified health professional.
modules.readingNote: CDC — Balancing Calories — for background reading on Energy Balance & Weight Management before the quiz and assignment
modules.videoNote: GIIS — Module 8: Energy Balance & Weight Management lesson video.
modules.practiceNote: Review CDC guidance on adolescent growth and healthy routines; identify when individualized concerns should be discussed with a parent, guardian, pediatrician, or registered dietitian.
modules.assignment: Submit: a one-page analysis of a provided media claim or fictional teen crash-diet scenario. Include: evidence about growth and sustainability, balanced growth-supporting alternatives, and when a parent, guardian, pediatrician, or registered dietitian should be consulted; personal weight or calorie targets are not required. Evaluation: the analysis identifies the claim's risks, cites course or qualified-source evidence, and proposes safe, realistic alternatives.

quizQuestions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the six classes of nutrients?
quizQuestions.answer: Enzymes
quizQuestions.explanation: The six classes of nutrients are carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals, and water. Enzymes are biological catalysts, not a nutrient class.

quizQuestions.question: Which nutrient class provides the most calories per gram?
quizQuestions.answer: Fat
quizQuestions.explanation: Fat provides 9 calories per gram, compared to 4 calories per gram for both carbohydrates and protein.

quizQuestions.question: Which nutrient supports fluid balance and temperature regulation without providing calories?
quizQuestions.answer: Water
quizQuestions.explanation: Water is an essential nutrient that supports transport, temperature regulation, and fluid balance but does not provide calories.

quizQuestions.question: Why is good nutrition especially important during adolescence?
quizQuestions.answer: Good nutrition supports rapid growth, brain development, energy, immune function, learning, activity, and long-term health patterns during adolescence.
quizQuestions.explanation: Adolescence is a major period of physical and cognitive development, so food quality affects both daily function and future health.

quizQuestions.question: Which food choice best represents a high-quality carbohydrate source for steady energy?
options: Oatmeal or whole-grain bread with fiber
Butter as the main energy source
quizQuestions.answer: Oatmeal or whole-grain bread with fiber
quizQuestions.explanation: High-quality carbohydrate sources provide energy along with fiber and nutrients, which support steadier blood sugar and longer-lasting fuel.

quizQuestions.question: Dietary fiber is best described as:
options: An indigestible carbohydrate that supports digestive health
quizQuestions.answer: An indigestible carbohydrate that supports digestive health
quizQuestions.explanation: Dietary fiber is a complex carbohydrate that humans cannot fully digest, supporting digestive health, satiety, and blood sugar regulation.

quizQuestions.question: The glycemic index measures:
options: The total carbohydrate content of a food
How quickly a food raises blood glucose levels
The amount of sugar in a product
quizQuestions.answer: How quickly a food raises blood glucose levels
quizQuestions.explanation: The glycemic index ranks foods by how quickly they raise blood sugar; high-GI foods cause rapid spikes, low-GI foods cause gradual rises.

quizQuestions.question: What is the primary function of carbohydrates in the body?
options: Providing energy (especially for the brain and during exercise)
quizQuestions.answer: Providing energy (especially for the brain and during exercise)
quizQuestions.explanation: Carbohydrates are the body's preferred energy source, especially for brain function and moderate-to-high intensity exercise.

quizQuestions.question: A complete protein contains:
options: Only essential amino acids from plants
All nine essential amino acids in adequate amounts
quizQuestions.answer: All nine essential amino acids in adequate amounts
quizQuestions.explanation: A complete protein provides all nine essential amino acids that the body cannot synthesize on its own.

quizQuestions.question: Which food source provides complete protein?
quizQuestions.answer: Eggs
quizQuestions.explanation: Eggs are a complete protein source containing all nine essential amino acids in adequate proportions.

quizQuestions.question: Which statement about protein needs for active teenagers is most accurate?
options: Needs vary with age, body size, growth, activity, health, and total diet
Every active teen needs exactly the same grams per kilogram
Protein needs depend only on height
Supplements are required to meet protein needs
quizQuestions.answer: Needs vary with age, body size, growth, activity, health, and total diet
quizQuestions.explanation: Qualified guidance considers the whole person and diet rather than applying one universal target.

quizQuestions.question: How can a vegetarian eating pattern provide all essential amino acids?
quizQuestions.answer: A varied vegetarian pattern can meet essential amino-acid needs through foods such as beans, lentils, soy, dairy or eggs when included, nuts, seeds, and grains across the day.
quizQuestions.explanation: Most students do not need to combine complementary proteins in the same meal; variety and adequate total intake across the day matter.

quizQuestions.question: Saturated fats are primarily found in:
quizQuestions.answer: Butter, red meat, and cheese
quizQuestions.explanation: Saturated fats are abundant in animal products like butter, red meat, and full-fat dairy, and are linked to elevated LDL cholesterol.

quizQuestions.question: Trans fats are most harmful because they:
options: Raise LDL (bad) cholesterol and lower HDL (good) cholesterol simultaneously
quizQuestions.answer: Raise LDL (bad) cholesterol and lower HDL (good) cholesterol simultaneously
quizQuestions.explanation: Trans fats raise LDL and lower HDL cholesterol, significantly increasing the risk of cardiovascular disease.

quizQuestions.question: Omega-3 fatty acids are especially beneficial for:
options: Heart health, brain function, and reducing inflammation
quizQuestions.answer: Heart health, brain function, and reducing inflammation
quizQuestions.explanation: Omega-3 fatty acids (EPA, DHA) reduce inflammation, support cardiovascular health, and promote brain development and function.

quizQuestions.question: Which substitution generally improves the dietary-fat pattern?
options: Replace a saturated fat with an unsaturated fat such as olive or canola oil
Replace water with a sugary drink
Replace vegetables with partially hydrogenated shortening
quizQuestions.answer: Replace a saturated fat with an unsaturated fat such as olive or canola oil
quizQuestions.explanation: Replacing saturated or trans fats with mono- or polyunsaturated fats can improve the overall fat pattern; dietary fat remains an essential nutrient.

quizQuestions.question: Which vitamins are fat-soluble?
options: Vitamins A, D, E, and K
quizQuestions.answer: Vitamins A, D, E, and K
quizQuestions.explanation: Fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) are stored in body fat and require dietary fat for absorption; B vitamins and C are water-soluble.

quizQuestions.question: Vitamin C deficiency causes which disease?
quizQuestions.answer: Scurvy
quizQuestions.explanation: Scurvy results from vitamin C deficiency, causing collagen breakdown, bleeding gums, poor wound healing, and fatigue.

quizQuestions.question: Why are vitamins A, D, E, and K grouped together?
options: They can only come from supplements
quizQuestions.answer: They are fat-soluble
quizQuestions.explanation: These vitamins dissolve in fat and can be stored in the body more readily than water-soluble vitamins.

quizQuestions.question: Which food is a useful source of vitamin C?
quizQuestions.answer: Orange or bell pepper
quizQuestions.explanation: Many fruits and vegetables, including citrus fruit and bell peppers, provide vitamin C.

quizQuestions.question: Calcium is most critical for which body function?
options: Bone and teeth formation and strength
quizQuestions.answer: Bone and teeth formation and strength
quizQuestions.explanation: Calcium is the primary mineral in bones and teeth, essential for their formation, density, and structural strength.

quizQuestions.question: Iron deficiency leads to which condition?
quizQuestions.answer: Iron-deficiency anemia
quizQuestions.explanation: Iron deficiency reduces hemoglobin production, impairing oxygen delivery and causing iron-deficiency anemia.

quizQuestions.question: Which food is the richest dietary source of calcium?
options: Dairy products like milk and yogurt
quizQuestions.answer: Dairy products like milk and yogurt
quizQuestions.explanation: Dairy products (milk, yogurt, cheese) are among the richest and most bioavailable sources of dietary calcium.

quizQuestions.question: What is one major role of iron in the body?
quizQuestions.answer: Helping hemoglobin carry oxygen
quizQuestions.explanation: Iron is required to make hemoglobin, the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen from the lungs to body tissues and supports normal energy metabolism.

quizQuestions.question: What health concern is associated with consistently excessive sodium intake?
quizQuestions.answer: Consistently excessive sodium intake is associated with higher blood pressure and increased cardiovascular risk, although individual needs and medical advice can vary.
quizQuestions.explanation: A strong answer links sodium with blood-pressure regulation without treating one food or one day as a diagnosis.

quizQuestions.question: Why does the percentage of water in the human body vary among people?
options: Age, body composition, sex, growth, and health can differ
Every person has exactly the same body-water percentage
Body water is unrelated to body composition
quizQuestions.answer: Age, body composition, sex, growth, and health can differ
quizQuestions.explanation: Body-water percentage varies across infancy, adolescence, adulthood, and different body compositions, so one fixed percentage should not be applied to everyone.

quizQuestions.question: Which of the following is an early sign of dehydration?
quizQuestions.answer: Dark yellow urine and thirst
quizQuestions.explanation: Dark urine and thirst are early indicators of mild dehydration before significant performance or health impairment occurs.

quizQuestions.question: Why is urine color only one clue, rather than a perfect test, of hydration?
options: Medicines, foods, supplements, and health conditions can also affect it
quizQuestions.answer: Medicines, foods, supplements, and health conditions can also affect it
quizQuestions.explanation: Hydration assessment uses context and multiple signs; urine color can be influenced by factors besides fluid intake.

quizQuestions.question: Which beverage is usually the best everyday choice for hydration, and why?
quizQuestions.answer: Plain water is usually the best everyday hydration choice because it replaces fluid without added sugar; individual needs can vary with activity, climate, and health.
quizQuestions.explanation: A strong answer identifies water and explains why special drinks are not generally needed for routine hydration.

quizQuestions.question: In Energy Balance & Weight Management, Energy balance means:
quizQuestions.answer: Calories consumed equal calories burned
quizQuestions.explanation: Energy balance occurs when caloric intake equals caloric expenditure, resulting in weight maintenance.

quizQuestions.question: Basal Metabolic Rate (BMR) refers to:
options: Calories burned at rest to maintain basic body functions
The rate at which food is digested
quizQuestions.answer: Calories burned at rest to maintain basic body functions
quizQuestions.explanation: BMR is the number of calories the body burns at rest to maintain basic physiological functions like breathing and circulation.

quizQuestions.question: A teenager is worried about weight and plans a severe calorie restriction. What is the safest next step?
options: Talk with a parent or guardian and a qualified health professional while focusing on growth-supporting habits
Begin a crash diet without telling anyone
Skip meals until the goal is reached
Copy an adult influencer's calorie target
quizQuestions.answer: Talk with a parent or guardian and a qualified health professional while focusing on growth-supporting habits
quizQuestions.explanation: Teenagers are still growing; individualized concerns should be discussed with trusted adults and qualified professionals rather than addressed through crash diets.

quizQuestions.question: Which factor can change a person's basal metabolic rate?
options: The color of a food package
The day of the month alone
quizQuestions.answer: Age, body composition, and growth
quizQuestions.explanation: BMR varies with factors such as age, body size and composition, growth, hormones, and health.

questions.question: Which of the six nutrient classes provides 9 calories per gram?
questions.answer: Fat
questions.explanation: Fat provides 9 calories per gram — more than twice the energy density of carbohydrates or protein (4 cal/g each).

questions.question: The glycemic index of a food indicates:
options: How rapidly it raises blood glucose levels
questions.answer: How rapidly it raises blood glucose levels
questions.explanation: The glycemic index measures how quickly a food raises blood sugar; high-GI foods cause rapid spikes.

questions.question: In Health and Nutrition midterm concepts, Complete proteins contain:
options: All nine essential amino acids in adequate amounts
questions.answer: All nine essential amino acids in adequate amounts
questions.explanation: Complete proteins supply all nine essential amino acids the body cannot make on its own.

questions.question: Why are trans fats considered especially harmful in nutrition education?
options: They can raise LDL cholesterol, lower HDL cholesterol, and increase heart disease risk
They are the main source of vitamin C
They are required for every meal
questions.answer: They can raise LDL cholesterol, lower HDL cholesterol, and increase heart disease risk
questions.explanation: Public health guidance generally recommends limiting trans fats because of their effect on blood cholesterol and cardiovascular risk.

questions.question: Which vitamin group is stored more readily in body fat than water-soluble vitamins?
questions.answer: A, D, E, and K
questions.explanation: Vitamins A, D, E, and K are fat-soluble, requiring dietary fat for absorption and stored in body fat.

questions.question: Iron deficiency primarily causes:
questions.answer: Iron-deficiency anemia
questions.explanation: Iron deficiency reduces hemoglobin production, resulting in iron-deficiency anemia with fatigue, pallor, and reduced oxygen transport.

questions.question: Which is an early sign of dehydration?
questions.answer: Early signs of dehydration can include thirst, dry mouth, darker urine, fatigue, headache, or reduced concentration.
questions.explanation: A strong response names observable early warning signs and connects them to the need to replace fluids before dehydration becomes more serious.

questions.question: Energy balance occurs when which relationship is roughly true?
options: Calories consumed roughly equal calories used
Calories consumed exceed calories used every day
questions.answer: Calories consumed roughly equal calories used
questions.explanation: Energy balance means intake and expenditure are approximately equal over time.

questions.question: Which choice best reflects current federal dietary guidance?
options: Build meals around varied nutrient-dense foods and reduce highly processed foods
Use supplements in place of meals
Choose foods only by package claims
questions.answer: Build meals around varied nutrient-dense foods and reduce highly processed foods
questions.explanation: Current guidance emphasizes nutrient-dense foods, variety, and reduced reliance on highly processed foods.

questions.question: When might a sports drink be useful instead of water alone?
options: During prolonged vigorous activity with substantial sweating, depending on conditions and individual needs
As the main beverage at every meal
Whenever a drink is brightly colored
questions.answer: During prolonged vigorous activity with substantial sweating, depending on conditions and individual needs
questions.explanation: Water is usually sufficient for routine activity; prolonged vigorous exercise, heavy sweating, heat, and individual needs can change fluid and electrolyte needs.

questions.question: Omega-3 fatty acids are primarily known for supporting:
options: Heart health, brain function, and reducing inflammation
questions.answer: Heart health, brain function, and reducing inflammation
questions.explanation: Omega-3 fatty acids (EPA and DHA) reduce inflammation and support cardiovascular health and brain function.

questions.question: Which description best identifies a complete protein food?
options: A food that provides all essential amino acids, such as eggs, dairy, meat, fish, soy, or quinoa
A food that contains only carbohydrates
A food with no amino acids
Any food that is low in calories
questions.answer: A food that provides all essential amino acids, such as eggs, dairy, meat, fish, soy, or quinoa
questions.explanation: Complete proteins contain all essential amino acids in meaningful amounts. This reinforces the Health and Nutrition midterm concepts idea behind the item instead of rewarding a surface-level guess.

questions.question: Dietary fiber's primary health benefit is:
options: Supporting digestive health, satiety, and blood sugar regulation
questions.answer: Supporting digestive health, satiety, and blood sugar regulation
questions.explanation: Dietary fiber promotes healthy digestion, reduces cholesterol absorption, supports blood sugar control, and increases satiety.

questions.question: Why is there no single daily fluid target that fits every active teenager?
questions.answer: Fluid needs vary with age, body size, activity intensity and duration, climate, diet, health, and sweat rate. A strong answer names several factors and explains that thirst and other signs provide context.
questions.explanation: Hydration guidance should account for individual and environmental differences rather than use one universal cup target.

questions.question: Calcium is most important during adolescence for:
options: Building peak bone mass for lifelong bone health
questions.answer: Building peak bone mass for lifelong bone health
questions.explanation: Adolescence is the critical window for peak bone mass development; adequate calcium intake during this period reduces lifelong osteoporosis risk.

questions.question: Which meal best applies current federal guidance to a student's lunch?
options: Vegetables, fruit, whole grains, and a varied protein source
Candy and soda as the entire meal
A meal selected only for low weight on the package
questions.answer: Vegetables, fruit, whole grains, and a varied protein source
questions.explanation: A varied nutrient-dense meal supplies several nutrient classes and supports sustainable eating patterns.

questions.question: Which action best supports a healthy relationship with food during adolescence?
options: Use regular, balanced meals and ask a qualified professional about individual concerns
Follow a severe restriction from social media
Skip meals to compensate for eating
Judge health from body size alone
questions.answer: Use regular, balanced meals and ask a qualified professional about individual concerns
questions.explanation: Growth-supporting habits and individualized professional guidance are safer than restrictive, appearance-driven plans.

questions.question: Why can two teenagers have different energy needs?
options: Growth, body size and composition, activity, and health can differ
One of them must be calculating incorrectly
Energy needs depend only on age
All teenagers have identical basal metabolic rates
questions.answer: Growth, body size and composition, activity, and health can differ
questions.explanation: Energy needs are individualized and reflect several biological and activity factors.

questions.question: Food waste in landfills contributes to climate change by producing:
questions.answer: Methane, a potent greenhouse gas
questions.explanation: Food decomposing without oxygen in landfills can produce methane, a potent greenhouse gas; the exact climate impact depends on time frame and waste-management conditions.

questions.question: Which change would most directly lower saturated-fat intake while preserving a source of dietary fat?
options: Replace butter with olive oil in a suitable recipe
questions.answer: Replace butter with olive oil in a suitable recipe
questions.explanation: Replacing a saturated fat with an unsaturated fat can improve the overall fat pattern.

questions.question: Which nutrient is uniquely produced by the body through sunlight exposure?
questions.answer: Vitamin D is the nutrient the body can produce when ultraviolet rays from sunlight reach the skin.
questions.explanation: Vitamin D can also come from foods or supplements, but this question focuses on the body's ability to synthesize vitamin D through sun exposure.

questions.question: After a long, vigorous practice, which snack best combines carbohydrate and protein?
questions.answer: Yogurt with fruit
questions.explanation: Carbohydrate helps replenish fuel and protein supports repair; individual needs vary with the activity and athlete.

questions.question: A student compares two breakfasts. Which evidence best supports the more nutrient-dense choice?
options: It provides fiber, protein, and several vitamins or minerals with limited added sugar
Its package uses the largest health claim
A celebrity recommends it without evidence
questions.answer: It provides fiber, protein, and several vitamins or minerals with limited added sugar
questions.explanation: Nutrient density compares useful nutrients with the overall food and eating pattern, not marketing alone.

questions.question: On a Nutrition Facts label, which section helps compare how much a nutrient contributes to a daily reference amount?
questions.answer: Percent Daily Value
questions.explanation: Percent Daily Value helps compare nutrient amounts across foods using a standard daily reference; individual needs may differ.

questions.question: A student has a one-hour routine practice in mild weather. Which hydration plan is usually appropriate?
options: Drink water before, during as needed, and after activity
Use an energy drink instead of water
questions.answer: Drink water before, during as needed, and after activity
questions.explanation: For routine activity, water and attention to thirst and conditions are generally appropriate.

questions.question: Which mineral is especially important for building bone during adolescence?
questions.answer: Calcium
questions.explanation: Adolescence is an important period for bone development, and calcium is a major bone mineral.

questions.question: Ingredients on a U.S. food label are listed in what order?
options: By weight from greatest to least
questions.answer: By weight from greatest to least
questions.explanation: Ingredient lists place the ingredient used in the greatest amount by weight first.

questions.question: Explain one way dietary fiber supports health.
questions.answer: Dietary fiber supports digestive regularity and can contribute to satiety, blood-glucose regulation, and heart health depending on the fiber and overall diet.
questions.explanation: A strong response accurately explains at least one function and connects it to a fiber-rich food or eating pattern.

questions.question: Which pattern is a warning sign that a teenager may need support from a trusted adult or health professional?
options: Repeated severe restriction, meal skipping, or distress about eating
questions.answer: Repeated severe restriction, meal skipping, or distress about eating
questions.explanation: Persistent restrictive behavior or distress around food deserves timely, supportive adult and professional attention.

questions.question: The Mediterranean diet's heart health benefits are largely attributed to:
options: High saturated fat from red meat
High fruit, vegetable, whole grain, legume, and olive oil intake
High sugar and processed food consumption
questions.answer: High fruit, vegetable, whole grain, legume, and olive oil intake
questions.explanation: The Mediterranean diet's cardiovascular benefits come from its high intake of anti-inflammatory plant foods and heart-healthy fats like olive oil.

questions.question: Which macronutrient has the highest caloric density?
questions.answer: Fat (9 cal/g)
questions.explanation: Fat provides 9 calories per gram, the highest energy density of any macronutrient.

questions.question: Severe vitamin C deficiency can lead to which condition?
questions.answer: Scurvy
questions.explanation: Vitamin C deficiency is classically associated with scurvy. Students need to recognize why Scurvy matches the evidence in the question and why nearby options do not.

questions.question: Which dietary pattern is generally associated with a lower environmental footprint, while recognizing that production methods vary?
questions.answer: Mostly plant-based foods
questions.explanation: Plant-forward dietary patterns are generally associated with lower greenhouse-gas impacts, although farming, processing, transport, and waste affect each food's lifecycle footprint.

questions.question: Basal Metabolic Rate (BMR) represents:
options: Calories burned at rest to maintain vital body functions
Total daily energy needs including all activity
Caloric intake from a typical meal
questions.answer: Calories burned at rest to maintain vital body functions
questions.explanation: BMR is the minimum energy the body needs at complete rest to sustain vital functions like breathing, circulation, and thermoregulation.

questions.question: Sodium's excessive intake is most associated with increased risk of:
questions.answer: Excessive sodium intake is most associated with increased risk of high blood pressure, which can raise risk for heart disease and stroke.
questions.explanation: This answer identifies the direct health concern, high blood pressure, and connects it to broader cardiovascular risk.
